# How to tell phpunit to stop on failure

Running a large test suite often feels like waiting for a marathon to finish before realizing you tripped in the first mile. By default, PHPUnit executes every test in your suite regardless of whether previous tests have failed. It only reports the failures at the very end, which can be frustrating when you need immediate feedback during development or debugging.

To change this behavior, you need to instruct PHPUnit to stop execution immediately upon encountering a failure. This is typically done by setting the `stop-on-failure` configuration option within your test suite setup.

## The Configuration Approach

The most robust way to enforce this behavior is through your PHPUnit XML configuration file, usually named `phpunit.xml`. You can add or modify the `<php>` section to include the specific attribute.

Add the following line inside the `<php>` tags of your `phpunit.xml`:

```xml
<php>
    <server name="STOP_ON_FAILURE" value="true"/>
</php>
```

Alternatively, you can set this directly within the `<testsuites>` or `<testdox>` sections depending on your specific version and setup, but placing it under the global `php` tag is generally safer as it applies to the entire test run. Once configured, PHPUnit will halt execution immediately after the first failing test case is encountered. This allows you to see exactly which file and line caused the issue without wasting time running hundreds of passing tests afterward.

## Command-Line Flags for Ad-Hoc Runs

Sometimes you might not want to permanently alter your configuration file, perhaps because you are running a specific subset of tests or debugging a transient environment issue. In these cases, PHPUnit supports command-line flags that achieve the same result without modifying files.

You can pass the `--stop-on-failure` flag directly when invoking the test runner:

```bash
vendor/bin/phpunit --stop-on-failure tests/
```

This approach is particularly useful in CI/CD pipelines or when you want to quickly verify if a specific change broke something without committing a config change to your repository. However, be aware that this flag applies only to the current invocation. If you run PHPUnit again later with different arguments, the default behavior (running all tests) will resume unless you add the flag again or update your configuration file.

## Understanding the Trade-Offs

While stopping on failure provides immediate feedback, it comes with a specific trade-off: you lose visibility into parallel failures. If multiple independent tests fail simultaneously, `--stop-on-failure` will report only the first one encountered. The rest of the failing tests are silently skipped because the process terminates early.

In a large suite, this can sometimes make debugging harder if you assume that only one test failed based on the output, but in reality, several might have crashed. If your goal is to fix a single bug quickly, stopping immediately is ideal. If your goal is to identify all regressions introduced by a commit before merging, running the full suite until completion provides a more accurate picture of the overall health of your codebase.

## Integration with Continuous Integration

When integrating this into a continuous integration environment like GitHub Actions or GitLab CI, you must weigh the speed benefits against the completeness of the report. Stopping on failure reduces pipeline execution time significantly if tests are slow. However, some teams prefer to run the full suite in CI to ensure nothing slips through the cracks, reserving `--stop-on-failure` for local development runs or specific debug steps within the pipeline where a test specifically fails and needs investigation.

## Final Considerations

If you are working within a Laravel project, you might also find it helpful to check how your existing test suite is configured. While Laravel simplifies many testing concerns, understanding these low-level PHPUnit options gives you granular control over the feedback loop. For teams looking for more advanced testing workflows or enterprise-grade testing solutions, exploring resources like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) can provide additional context on best practices beyond basic PHPUnit configuration.

Ultimately, the decision to stop on failure depends on your workflow. For rapid iteration and fixing specific bugs, it is an excellent tool. For comprehensive regression analysis, running the full suite remains necessary.
